Cesar Malan
sā'-zar ma-lan'
n. (Cesar Malan, 1787–1864, Genevan preacher and hymnwriter, a founder of the Reveil)
Latin Caesar, a Roman family name; Malan, a Waldensian surname, from the Piedmontese valleys.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Cesar Malan was a regent of the college at Geneva, of Waldensian descent, who in 1816 preached a sermon on justification by faith alone before the Venerable Company of Pastors and was dismissed from his post for it. Geneva's established church had by then settled into a polite Socinianism in which the deity of Christ was not denied so much as never mentioned, and Malan's preaching of the ruin of man and free grace in Christ was taken as fanaticism. He built a chapel in his own garden, the Chapelle du Temoignage, was suspended from the ministry of the national church in 1823, and spent forty years preaching there and travelling through France, Belgium, Scotland and England. With the Haldanes' influence and alongside Merle d'Aubigne and the Monod brothers he was a founder of the Reveil, the Francophone evangelical awakening. He wrote over a thousand hymns, many still sung in French Protestant churches, and among his converts was John Duncan of Edinburgh. “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a revival as renewed attention to religion after decline, and a hymn as a song in honour of God.

REVI'VAL, n. Renewed attention to religion, after indifference and decline.

HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God; a sacred lyric.

SUSPEND', v.t. To debar from any privilege, or from the execution of an office, for a time.

Modern Corruption

The Genevan dismissed in 1816 for preaching justification by faith, and founder of the Reveil.

expand to see more

Malan's Geneva is the standing example of how a church loses the gospel without ever voting against it. No synod repudiated the deity of Christ or the atonement; the Company of Pastors simply agreed in 1817 that these subjects should not be treated in the pulpit, in the interest of peace. A generation of Genevans grew up hearing moral instruction in Calvin's own city.

The principle to recover is that silence on the central things is itself a denial, and that the apostolic answer to an order of silence is not negotiation: “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20). The gospel is the power of God unto salvation (Rom 1:16), and a pulpit that will not name it has nothing else to offer.
